podcast.title: Invention of Moog Synthesizer (1965)
podcast.body: Dr. Robert Moog invented the Moog synthesizer in 1965, a crucial development because previous synthesizers were unwieldy, huge (the size of railway cars), heat-generating, and programmable only with hundreds of patch cords. While still ungainly, Moog's invention was more manageable in size, allowing more musicians to experiment. "That's when Dr. Robert Mogue invented the Mogue synthesizer. This is very important because up until then, synthesizers were honestly the size of railway cars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Invention of Mini Moog (1971)
podcast.body: In 1971, Dr. Moog introduced the Mini Moog, an invention credited with making much of today's music possible. This synthesizer could perform almost everything its larger predecessors could, but was significantly smaller (a little bigger than a suitcase) and, crucially, much cheaper, making the technology accessible to a new generation of musicians, many of whom came of age during the punk era. "The big break came in 1971 when Dr. Mogue showed up again, this time with a new synthesizer design he called the Mini Mogue. This one invention made much of today's music possible."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Concern for Moog Company's Future
podcast.body: Bob Moog expressed concern that his company was facing imminent doom if they failed to innovate and produce something significantly different from the existing giant modular synthesizers. This motivated the development of the Mini-Moog. "Bob Mogen, as people knew, if they didn't come up with something different, the company was doomed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inventor of the Synthesizer
podcast.body: Bob Moog is recognized as the inventor of the synthesizer. His new machines captivated Malcolm Cecil and Robert Margouleff in the late 1960s, inspiring them to build TONTO, the massive modular synth that profoundly influenced electronic music. "These guys, a British jazz dude working for the BBC and an American record producer, were huge influences on the world of electronic music, but they were almost entirely behind the scenes."

xref.title: A Clockwork Orange (1972) Score
xref.body: Wendy Carlos, a classical musician who had been collaborating with Bob Moog on the development and application of his new modular synthesizers, was hired by director Stanley Kubrick to compose the score for his 1971 futuristic dystopian film, *A Clockwork Orange*. The entirely electronic score, released as a soundtrack in 1972 (with Carlos identifying as Walter Carlos at the time), introduced sounds no one had heard before and became a landmark in the widespread development of electronic music, influencing many rock musicians seeking novel sounds. "No one had ever heard such sounds. It was completely electronic."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Collaboration with Bob Moog
xref.body: Carlos worked closely with Bob Moog at the Columbia-Princeton Electronic Music Center, where she offered a crucial musician's perspective on the design and feel of his new electronic instruments. Her input was instrumental in decisions like incorporating a keyboard and refining the tactile experience of individual keys, making synthesizers more user-friendly for musicians. "She worked carefully with Bob Mogue, offering a musician's perspective, and how his new electronic instruments should look and feel."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Collaboration with Bob Moog and Film Score Work
xref.body: Wendy Carlos worked directly with synthesizer pioneer Bob Moog, using his innovative instruments. This collaboration led her to create the first all-synthesizer soundtrack for Stanley Kubrick's seminal futuristic film, *A Clockwork Orange*, demonstrating the significant artistic potential of the new technology. "That's from Wendy Carlos, who worked with Bob Mogue on his synthesizer. We created the All-Synth Soundtrack for Stanley Kubrick's futuristic Ecluckwork Orange."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneering Electronic Music with TONTO
xref.body: In the late 1960s, Malcolm Cecil, a British jazz musician working for the BBC, along with American record producer Robert Margouleff, were fascinated by new synthesizers from Bob Moog. They set out to construct the world's largest modular synth setup, which they named TONTO (The Original New Timbral Orchestra). This behemoth, comprising gear from Moog, Oberheim, ARP, EMS, Roland, and Yamaha, allowed for unprecedented sound creation and multi-track performance, profoundly influencing electronic music. "These guys, a British jazz dude working for the BBC and an American record producer, were huge influences on the world of electronic music, but they were almost entirely behind the scenes."

xref.title: Pioneering Electronic Music with TONTO
xref.body: In the late 1960s, American record producer Robert Margouleff, alongside British jazz musician Malcolm Cecil, was captivated by Bob Moog's new synthesizers. They embarked on creating TONTO (The Original New Timbral Orchestra), the world's largest modular synth setup. This colossal instrument, built with components from various manufacturers, enabled unprecedented sonic textures and multi-layered compositions, significantly impacting electronic music production. "These guys, a British jazz dude working for the BBC and an American record producer, were huge influences on the world of electronic music, but they were almost entirely behind the scenes."
